INTRODUCTION
At the manufacturing facility of Emery Oleochemicals LLC in Cincinnati, Ohio, safeguarding the well-being of employees, the community, and the environment is regarded as the highest priority. A fundamental aspect of the plant's safety program involves creating and executing strategies aimed at preventing unintentional chemical releases. Furthermore, in the event of an accidental release, the plant staff is trained to respond in a systematic and efficient manner.
The plant's accident prevention and emergency response programs have been developed in accordance with federal and state regulations, industry standards, and guidance from local emergency response organizations.
The Risk Management Program (RMP) at the plant was developed to meet federal regulations aimed at preventing accidental chemical releases, as outlined in 40 CFR 68, Chemical Accident Prevention Provisions. This regulation seeks to minimize the risk of such incidents and enhance emergency response strategies both at the facility and within the surrounding community. The RMP details potential catastrophic events, referred to as "worst-case release scenarios," alongside various less severe "alternative release scenarios." While the worst-case scenarios are deemed technically improbable, their inclusion serves to bolster emergency preparedness. Consequently, this proactive approach ensures that the community is equipped to effectively handle more likely, lower-magnitude incidents.
Areas that could be impacted by an accidental chemical release were identified using RMP*Comp (Ver 1.07), which was developed by U. S. EPA for accidental chemical release modeling.

EMERY OLEOCHEMICALS LLC
Cognis Corporation carved out the Fatty Acid, Glycerine, Ozone Acids and Plastics Technology Businesses creating Cognis Oleochemicals LLC in January 2006.  In May 2009, the company name was changed to Emery Oleochemicals LLC.
The Emery Oleochemicals LLC manufacturing facility is certified under the ISO 14000 Envi

ronmental Management System Standard.

ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION AND RESPONSE POLICIES
The policy at Emery Oleochemicals LLC Cincinnati plant is to prevent all releases of potentially harmful substances.  Senior management is responsible for release prevention and response programs, and considerable time and resources have been invested in this effort.  
The plant has detailed procedures to ensure that safety is considered in the design, installation, operation and maintenance of each process.  Plant personnel receive regular safety training, and employee input is solicited on every aspect of safety performance improvement.  Failure to follow safety policies is grounds for dismissal.
If a release were to occur, trained personnel would control and contain the release.  The standard procedure is to technically evaluate each situation, identify potential on-site and off-site impacts, evacuate or shelter employees as necessary, contain the release and contact the local fire department to control the release and minimize its consequences.

DESCRIPTION OF STATIONARY SOURCE 
The Emery Oleochemicals LLC Cincinnati, Ohio plant is a chemical manufacturing facility located at 4900 Este Avenue.  A variety of processes are operated at the plant to produce products derived from animal fat or vegetable oil.  The plant, originally constructed in 1885, is situated on 40 acres of land. Part of the plant is located in the City of Cincinnati and part is located in the City of St. Bernard.  The two parts are separated by the Mill Creek, a tributary of the Ohio River.  Fatty Acids, Glycerine and Ozone Acids are the major products produced at the Cincinnati plant. In 2015 Emery Oleochemicals added batch reactors for the manufacture of fatty acid based esters and polyols.  Neither of the new processes are regulated under the RMP standards.
The plant is subject to numerous environmental, health and safety regulations and is regularly inspected by agency representatives.  The following a

ctivities are specifically regulated:
	Air emissions - permits issued by Ohio EPA including a Title V operating permit, 
	Hazardous chemical emissions reduction - US EPA MON MACT standard and OEPA RACT standards
	Wastewater - discharge permits issued by Ohio EPA and the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati,
	Oil spill prevention - subject to OPA-90 regulations,
	Storm water - permit issued by Ohio EPA,
	Hazardous waste management - U. S. EPA ID# OHD093903235,
	Process safety - subject to OSHA Process Safety Management and US EPA Risk Management Program rules,
	General workplace safety - subject to OSHA 1910 general industry regulations,
	Transportation of hazardous goods - Dept of Transporation (DOT) regulations,
	Chemical risk management - US EPA Toxic Substance Control Act (TSCA) standards,
	Emergency planning - subject to SARA 311/312 reporting, and
	Toxic chemical release reporting - subject to SARA 313 reporting (ID # 45232 HNKLC4900E).

DESCRIPTION OF REGULATED SUBSTANCES
The Cincinnati plant handles two chemicals in sufficient quantities to be covered by the RMP regulations.  Ammonia, which is regulated as toxic substance, is used as a refrigerant in the Solvent Separation process.  Hydrogen, which is regulated as a flammable substance, is used as a process ingredient in the Hydrogenation processes that are part of the Stearic Acid manufacturing operations.  All of these processes have been assigned to RMP Program Level 3.
NOTE: The reporting of this Hydrogen system is a duplicate reporting. The system has also been reported by Air Products, Inc. (EPA ID # 1000 0001 8358). The system is completely owned, operated and maintained by Air Products but is located on property owned by Emery Oleochemicals and BASF Corp. The Hydrogen stored within the system is supplied to the Emery Oleochemicals LLC facility. The dual reporting is by mutual consent of both companies.

OFFSITE CONSEQUENCE ANALYSIS 
Following U. S. EPA guidance, an offsite con

sequence analysis (OCA) was performed to determine the potential for an accidental release of a regulated substance to affect the public or the environment.  The OCA included both worst-case release scenarios (WCSs) and alternative release scenarios (ARSs).  Considering the design of the regulated processes and the plant's accident prevention programs, it is virtually impossible for the WCSs to occur.  Although it is highly unlikely that the ARSs would ever occur, the ARSs represent release scenarios that are at least somewhat feasible. 
The main objective of the OCA was to determine the furthest distance (called the endpoint distance) at which certain conditions might exist as a result of an accidental chemical release.  Most people at the endpoint distance would be able to walk away from the exposure without any long-term health consequences, although some short-term consequences are possible.

FIVE-YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY
On March 6, 2023, at approximately 6:57:51 PM, a hydrogen leak in the compressor room of Building 81, Continuous Hydrogenation, ignited, causing damage within the room and affecting other areas of the building as well as several nearby structures. Fortunately, there were no injuries reported on-site or off-site, and while there were no external impacts, the explosion's sound was audible from several miles away. All required notification were made at the time of the event. Additionally, a later report was filed with the Chemical Safety Board (CSB) due to damage cost.

GENERAL ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION PROGRAM STEPS
The following is a summary of the general accident prevention program in place at the Cincinnati plant.  Since processes at the plant that are regulated under the RMP regulations are also subject to the OSHA Process Safety Management (PSM) standard, this summary addresses each of the OSHA PSM elements and describes the management system in place to implement the accident prevention program.

Employee Participation
The Cincinnati plan

t actively promotes employee involvement in all aspects of process safety management and accident prevention. Employees can engage in various activities, such as updating technical documents and chemical information, as well as serving on process hazard analysis (PHA) teams. They have full access to all materials related to the facility's accident prevention program, with specific participation methods outlined in an employee participation plan that covers each element of the program. In 2023, the plant introduced the SafeStart initiative to enhance safety discussions and facilitate the sharing of lessons learned among staff. This program includes a financial incentive for employees who share personal experiences related to safety incidents, with a guarantee that no disciplinary action will be taken against them unless the event was intentional and violated the facility's life-saving rules. Additionally, every Wednesday at noon, teams gather in designated areas to discuss a Health, Safety, or Environmental (HSE) message prepared by the HSE department, which reviews past HSE events and focuses on relevant safety topics applicable to work, home, and travel.

Process Safety Information
The Cincinnati plant keeps a variety of technical documents that are used to help maintain safe operation of the processes.  These documents address chemical properties and associated hazards, limits for key process parameters and specific chemical inventories, and equipment design basis/configuration information.  Specific departments within the plant are assigned responsibility for maintaining up-to-date process safety information.  A table summarizing the reference documents, and their location is readily available as part of the written employee participation plan to help employees locate any necessary process safety information.
Chemical-specific information, including exposure hazards and emergency response/exposure treatment considerations, is provided in material safety data shee

ts. This information is supplemented by documents that specifically address known hazards. For specific process areas, the plant has documented safety-related limits for certain process parameters (e.g., temperature, level, composition) maintained in the process operating procedures.  The plant ensures that the process is maintained within these limits using process controls and monitoring instruments, highly trained personnel, and protective instrument systems (e.g., automated shutdown systems).
The plant also maintains numerous technical documents that provide information about the design and construction of process equipment.  The information includes materials of construction, design pressure and temperature ratings, electrical rating of equipment, etc. This information, in combination with written procedures and trained personnel, provides a basis for establishing inspection and maintenance activities, as well as for evaluating proposed process and facility changes to ensure that safety features in the process are not compromised.

Process Hazard Analysis
The facility has implemented a thorough program designed to identify and manage hazards associated with its various processes. This program involves a systematic review of each process to pinpoint potential hazards and ensure that appropriate controls are established to mitigate these risks. Starting in 2024, safeguards will be categorized based on the Layer of Protection (LOP) they provide. The term "PHA safeguards categories" refers to the different classifications of safety measures identified during a Process Hazard Analysis (PHA), which are intended to prevent or reduce the likelihood of hazardous incidents in industrial operations. Emery utilizes eight specific categories to classify these safeguards, with each category serving as an Independent Layer of protection.
Safeguard Categories: 
1.	Inherent Design refers to the design of equipment and processes that specifically accommodate the parameters expec

ted during both normal and abnormal operations. 
2.	Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS) consist of safety mechanisms that include sensors, logic solvers, and final control elements, which are intended to bring the process to a safe state when specific predetermined conditions are breached.   SIS are independently connected to a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC). 
3.	Basic Process Control Systems (BPCS) and Process Interlocks are responsible for monitoring and controlling the process to ensure it remains within established normal parameters. For instance, Solvent D utilizes the Delta V Process Control System. 
4.	Alarms or Operators are preconfigured to notify operators when a parameter has been exceeded, prompting them to take necessary corrective actions based on the deviation. 
5.	Administrative Controls, Procedures, and Training encompass safety measures that involve the establishment of clear guidelines, provision of adequate training for employees, and implementation of standardized work practices to reduce personnel and process hazards. 
6.	Active Physical Protection Systems are designed to function automatically when physical parameters are surpassed, without requiring intervention from process controls or operators. These systems include pressure safety valves and rupture discs. 
7.	Passive Protection Systems aim to lessen the impact of an event after it has occurred. Examples of these systems include fire protection measures, containment dikes, blast walls, and personal protective equipment (PPE). 
8.	Emergency Response involves trained on-site or off-site responders who are prepared to manage incidents such as fires, chemical releases and medical emergencies.
Additionally, beginning in 2024, all PHA's specifically cover causes, impacts, and safeguards regarding loss of plant air, nitrogen, steam, and electricity as well as possible impacts of extreme nature events.
The plant primarily uses a hazard and operability (HAZOP) analysis technique to perform thes

e evaluations.  HAZOP analysis is recognized as one of the most systematic and thorough hazard evaluation techniques.  The analysis is led by a trained PHA facilitator.  The PHA teams consist of people who have operating and maintenance experience as well as engineering expertise. The team identifies and evaluates the hazards associated with a process as well as accident prevention and mitigation measures and makes suggestions for additional prevention and/or mitigation measures when the team believes such measures are necessary.
The findings from the Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) team are submitted to both local and corporate management for resolution. The implementation of mitigation strategies is guided by a risk ranking assigned by the PHA team, ensuring that the most critical accident scenarios receive prompt attention. All approved mitigation measures are monitored until their completion, and the final outcomes of each finding are documented and preserved. 
To maintain alignment with the original safety design features, the plant conducts periodic updates and revalidations of the hazard analysis results at least every five years, continuing this practice until the process is decommissioned. The outcomes of these reviews are also documented and retained.
Operating Procedures
The facility has established documented procedures that cover various operational modes, including unit startup, routine operations, temporary operations, emergency shutdowns, normal shutdowns, and the initial startup of new processes. These procedures serve as a valuable reference for seasoned operators and form the foundation for consistent training of new personnel. They undergo regular reviews and are certified annually to ensure they remain current and accurate. Updates are made as needed through the Management of Change (MOC) process to reflect any modifications. Furthermore, the operating procedures offer essential guidance for responding to unexpected situations, such as electrical

outages or process alarms. This information, along with the written procedures, is easily accessible to operators within the process unit and is also provided to other staff members to ensure safe execution of their job responsibilities.
Training
To enhance the written procedures for process operations, the plant has established a thorough training program for all personnel engaged in operational tasks. New hires receive foundational training in plant operations if they lack prior experience. Upon completing this initial training, they are paired with experienced operators to acquire knowledge of specific process duties. Once operators demonstrate their competence through assessments and practical evaluations, they are permitted to work independently. Additionally, all operators undergo refresher training on operating procedures at least every three years to ensure their skills and knowledge remain current. Documentation of all training activities, including verification of understanding, is maintained for each operator.

Contractors
The plant uses contractors to supplement its workforce during periods of increased maintenance or construction activities or for specialized maintenance work.  Because some contractors work on or near process equipment, the plant has procedures in place to ensure that contractors:
	Perform their work in a safe manner, 
	Have the appropriate knowledge and skills,
	Are aware of the hazards in their workplace,
	Understand what they should do in the event of an emergency,
	Understand and follow site safety rules, and 
	Inform plant personnel of any hazards that they find during their work.
This is accomplished by providing contractors with the necessary training prior to beginning their work.  In addition, the plant evaluates contractor safety programs and performance during the selection of a contractor.  Plant personnel periodically monitor contractor performance to ensure that contractors are fulfilling their safety obligations.
Pr

e-startup Safety Reviews (PSSR's)
The plant conducts a PSSR for any new facility or major modification of an existing facility. The purpose of the PSSR is to ensure that safety features, procedures, personnel, and the equipment are appropriately prepared for startup prior to placing the equipment into service.  This review provides one additional check to make sure construction is in accordance with the design specifications and that all supporting systems are operationally ready.  The PSSR review team uses checklists to verify all aspects of readiness.  A PSSR involves field verification of the construction and serves a quality assurance function by requiring verification that accident prevention program requirements are properly implemented. 
PSSR's are also conducted after the completion of Maintenance Turnaround. The Maintenance Turnaround PSSR is completed before maintenance is released from the shutdown and before the plant is restarted. 
Mechanical Integrity
The plant has well-established practices and procedures to maintain pressure vessels, piping systems, relief and vent systems, process controls, pumps and compressors, valves and emergency shutdown systems in a safe operating condition.  The basic elements of this program include:
	Conducting training,
	Developing written procedures,
	Performing inspections and tests,
	Correcting identified deficiencies, and
	Applying quality assurance measures.
In combination, these activities form a system that maintains the mechanical integrity of the process equipment.
Maintenance personnel receive training on an overview of the process, safety and health hazards, applicable maintenance procedures, emergency response plans, and applicable safe work practices to help ensure that they can perform their jobs in a safe manner.  Written procedures help ensure that work is performed in a consistent manner and provide a basis for training.  Inspections and tests are performed to help ensure that equipment functions as i

ntended, and to verify that equipment is within acceptable limits (e.g., adequate wall thickness for pressure vessels).  If a deficiency is identified, employees will correct the deficiency before placing the equipment back into service (if possible), or an MOC team will review the use of the equipment and determine what actions are necessary to ensure the safe operation of the equipment.
Another integral part of the mechanical integrity program is quality assurance.  The plant incorporates quality assurance measures into equipment purchases and repairs.  This helps ensure that the new equipment is suitable for its intended use and that proper material and spare parts are used when repairs are made.
Safe Work Practices
The Cincinnati plant has long-standing safe work practices in place to help ensure worker and process safety.  Examples of these include:
	Control of the entry/presence/exit of support personnel,
	Permit and procedure for lockout/tagout to ensure isolation of energy sources for equipment undergoing maintenance,
	Procedure for safe removal of hazardous materials before process piping or equipment is opened,
	Permit and procedure to control spark-producing activities (i.e., hot work),
	Permit and procedure to ensure that adequate precautions are in place before entry into a confined space,
	Permit and procedure for any excavation work,
	Personal protective equipment standards based on the type of hazards workers may encounter,
	Hazard Communication Program,
	Hazardous Chemical safe handling procedures, and
	Checklists and procedures for loading and unloading tank trucks and rail cars.      
These procedures (and others), along with training of affected personnel, form a system to help ensure that operations and maintenance activities are performed safely.

Management of Change
The plant has a comprehensive system to manage changes to processes.  This system requires that changes to items such as process equipment, chemicals, technology (includ

ing process operating conditions), procedures, and other facility changes be properly reviewed and authorized before being implemented.  Changes are reviewed to ensure that adequate controls are in place to manage any new hazards and to verify that existing controls have not been compromised by the change.  Affected chemical hazard information, process operating limits, and equipment information, as well as procedures, are updated to incorporate these changes.  In addition, operating and maintenance personnel are provided any necessary training on the change.

Incident Investigation
The plant conducts thorough investigations into all incidents that have caused or could potentially cause a fire, explosion, toxic gas release, significant property damage, environmental harm, or OSHA recordable injuries. Each investigation aims to uncover the facts and formulate corrective measures to prevent similar occurrences in the future. The investigation team meticulously documents their findings and recommendations, which are then submitted to plant management for action. The implementation of corrective measures is monitored until completion, and the final outcomes of each recommendation are recorded. Additionally, the investigation results are shared with all employees, including contractors, who may be impacted by the findings. Incident investigation reports are preserved for a minimum of five years to facilitate review during future Process Hazard Analyses (PHAs) and PHA revalidations.
Compliance Audits
To help ensure that the accident prevention program is functioning properly, the Cincinnati plant periodically conducts an audit to determine whether the procedures and practices required by the accident prevention program are being implemented.  A compliance audit is conducted at least once every three years.  The audit team develops findings that are forwarded to plant management for resolution.  Corrective action plans developed in response to the audit team's findings are

tracked until all items are complete.  The final resolution of each finding is documented, and the two most recent reports are retained.
Due to the hydrogen event in 2023, the 2026, compliance audit will be conducted by a third party 

CHEMICAL- SPECIFIC PREVENTION STEPS
The processes at the Cincinnati plant have hazards that must be managed to ensure continued safe operation.  The accident prevention program summarized previously is applied to all RMP-covered processes at the facility.  Collectively, these prevention program activities help prevent potential accidental scenarios that could be caused by equipment failure or human error.
In addition to the accident prevention program activities, the Cincinnati plant has safety features on many units to help detect, contain/control, and reduce the consequences of a release.  The following types of safety features are used in various processes:
Release Detection
	Chemical detectors with alarms. In 2025, new anhydrous ammonia sensors equipped with alarms were tested successfully. These advanced sensors are designed to function effectively in high-moisture environments, such as those with steam, without being adversely affected. Following the positive results from the trial, plans are underway to install these sensors in two anhydrous ammonia plants. A Management of Change (MOC) process was initiated for both the trial and the subsequent permanent installation.
	Release Containment/Control
	Scrubbers to neutralize or cool process vent streams prior to release to the environment,
	Valves to permit isolation of the process (manual and automated),
	Automated shutdown systems to a process if an upset condition occurs (e.g., high level, high temperature),
	Curbing or diking to contain liquid releases,
	Redundant equipment and instrumentation,
	Emergency backup power supply for critical controls,
	Special classified electrical equipment in areas where flammable chemicals are used,
	Release Mitigation
	Fire suppress

ion and extinguishing systems,
	Trained emergency response personnel,
	Personal protective equipment (e.g., protective clothing, self-contained breathing apparatus), and
	Blast-resistant buildings and windows to help protect control systems and personnel.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM INFORMATION
The Cincinnati facility has established a comprehensive written emergency response program designed to safeguard the health and safety of both employees and the surrounding community, as well as to protect the environment. This program outlines specific procedures for managing incidents involving the release of regulated substances, including potential fire or explosion risks associated with flammable materials. It encompasses all facets of emergency response, such as administering first aid and medical care for exposure incidents, implementing evacuation strategies, ensuring personnel accountability post-evacuation, notifying local emergency services in the event of a release, and conducting post-incident cleanup and decontamination. Furthermore, the plant has protocols for the maintenance, inspection, and testing of emergency response equipment, along with guidelines for its proper use. Employees are trained in these procedures as needed to fulfill their emergency response roles, and the program is regularly updated to reflect any changes in plant processes or facilities.
The emergency response program at the Cincinnati plant is effectively managed in collaboration with the Hamilton County Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC), as well as the fire departments of Cincinnati and St. Bernard, along with other local businesses. The facility maintains continuous communication with relevant LEPC officials and emergency response teams, ensuring prompt public notification in the event of an incident and enabling swift action when necessary. In addition to regular LEPC meetings, the plant organizes emergency drills that engage both the LEPC and local emergency responders, whi

le also providing ongoing training to these responders about the potential hazards associated with the regulated substances present at the facility.

ADDITIONAL EMERGENCY CONTACTS (supplement to Section 1.8)
Emery Oleochemicals LLC, Cincinnati plant has a total of eight (8) Shift Supervisors that, while they are on duty, have the responsibility of being the Emergency Contact. The additional Shift Supervisors that serve as Emergency Contacts are as follows:
The Primary Emergency Response Incident Commander is the on-shift OZONE Shift Supervisor.
The Back-up Emergency Response Incident Commander is the on-shift Fatty Acids Shift Supervisor.
